title: Cross-Layer Feature Routing for Harm: Do Earlier Layers Set Up Later-Layer Safety Bypasses?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: finding that jailbreaks manipulate early-layer features that cascade to disable safety heads would shift safety system architecture toward early-layer monitoring, but the chain from finding to deployed monitoring system has a gap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: SAE feature analysis at early layers and causal patching of those features into refused prompts is intermediate TransformerLens work. Comparing successful vs failed jailbreaks requires careful curation but is technically manageable.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: curating successful/failed jailbreak pairs, computing early-layer SAE features, identifying differentiating features, and running causal patching propagation experiments. Multiple experimental phases.

novelty.reasoning: Several works have investigated cross-layer jailbreak mechanisms. 'Jailbreaks Peak Early, Then Drop' (LessWrong 2025) studied layer trajectories showing jailbreak signals peak in mid-layers then decrease. 'JailbreakLens' (arXiv:2411.11114) combines representation and circuit analysis to reveal how jailbreaks penetrate layer by layer. 'In-Context Representation Hijacking' (arXiv:2512.03771) showed semantic hijacking occurs progressively across layers. 'Subspace Rerouting' used mechanistic interpretability to craft adversarial attacks. The specific framing of early-layer SAE features causally propagating to disable later safety heads is a more granular mechanistic hypothesis not yet directly tested, but the broader phenomenon of cross-layer jailbreak propagation is well-studied.
